title: Cookies, Sessions & State
objectives: Describe how Set-Cookie and Cookie carry state across stateless HTTP
Choose between server-side sessions and stateless signed tokens
Harden cookies with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite attributes
body:
# Cookies, Sessions & State

## The problem
HTTP is stateless: every request arrives with no memory of the last. Yet a shop must remember a cart and a login must survive navigation. The classic fix is handing the client a small token (a cookie) and keeping state keyed by that token. Where that state lives - and how much the cookie reveals - is a security and scaling decision.

## Cookies 101
The server sets a cookie with `Set-Cookie`; the browser echoes it back in `Cookie` on later requests to that scope:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: sid=9f3ac2; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=86400
```

Attributes that matter:
- `Expires` / `Max-Age`: session cookie (gone on browser close) vs persistent.
- `Domain` / `Path`: scoping; narrower is safer.
- `HttpOnly`: invisible to JavaScript, which blunts XSS token theft.
- `Secure`: sent only over HTTPS.
- `SameSite=Lax|Strict|None`: cross-site sending policy, the first line of CSRF defense.

## Where should session state live?
- Server-side: the cookie holds an opaque `sid`; the server maps `sid -> {userId, roles}` in Redis or memory. Instantly revocable, and the cookie stays tiny.
- Stateless: the cookie (or header) carries a signed token (JWT) with claims baked in. No shared store and easy to scale, but revocation means waiting for expiry or maintaining a denylist.

## Tradeoffs
| | Server-side | Signed token |
|---|---|---|
| Revocation | instant | wait or denylist |
| Shared store | required | not required |
| Cookie size | tiny | grows with claims |
| Cross-service auth | needs shared store | works anywhere |

## Decision framework
- Browser app, one backend, logout must work? -> opaque sid plus a server-side store.
- Many independent services, short-lived access? -> signed token with a short Max-Age plus refresh rotation.
- Either way: `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite=Lax` are the baseline.

## Best practices
- Use one session cookie holding a random 128-bit+ value; never trust client-stored roles without a signature.
- Rotate the session id at login to defeat session fixation.
- Expire server sessions with a sliding TTL and purge stale ones.
- Keep `Domain` unset so the cookie stays on the exact host that set it.

## Common mistakes
- Storing roles or PII in a plain unsigned cookie - trivially forged with devtools.
- Missing `HttpOnly`, letting any XSS read the session token.
- `SameSite=None` without `Secure`, which modern browsers reject outright.
- Debugging with `document.cookie` and concluding cookies are broken because `HttpOnly` hides them by design.

examples.name: login-flow.sh
examples.code:
# Log in and keep the session cookie in a jar
curl -s -c cookies.txt -X POST https://api.example.com/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"user":"ada","pass":"s3cret"}'

# Reuse it; the session id travels automatically
curl -s -b cookies.txt https://api.example.com/me

exercise.prompt: Implement missingFlags(header, required): given a Set-Cookie header value, return the list of required flags (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) that are missing. Matching must be case-insensitive.
hints: Case-insensitive matching keeps this simple: lowercase both sides before checking.
String.includes is enough here; each flag appears verbatim when present.
This unhardened cookie is missing all three flags.

questions.prompt: Which cookie attribute stops JavaScript from reading the session cookie?
questions.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie and other script access, blunting XSS-based token theft.

questions.prompt: Why is SameSite=None without Secure rejected by modern browsers?
options: It makes the cookie too large
Cross-site cookies must only travel over HTTPS
questions.explanation: None opts the cookie into cross-site sending, so browsers require the Secure flag to keep it off plaintext connections.

questions.prompt: What is the main tradeoff of stateless signed-token sessions versus server-side sessions?
options: They cannot be used in browsers
They are hard to revoke before expiry
questions.explanation: Self-contained tokens need no shared store but cannot be instantly revoked; server-side sessions revoke instantly at the cost of shared state.
